lessons.title: Why Levels Exist — The Market's Order Memory
lessons.summary: Explain in plain English why price keeps reacting at the same areas, and use that explanation to judge which areas are likely to matter again.
lessons.html:
Open any chart, on any pair, on any timeframe, and you will see it within a minute. Price falls to an area, turns, wanders away, comes back weeks later — and turns again from almost exactly the same place. It looks like the chart has a memory. It looks, frankly, a bit like magic.

It isn't magic, and the reason matters. If you only know that levels work, you will draw them everywhere and trust them equally. If you know why they work, you can tell the difference between an area where real orders are likely still waiting and an area that simply has a line on it because you put one there.

This course teaches a complete, practical method for support and resistance: how to find the areas that matter, draw them honestly as zones, rank them, read what price does when it arrives, and plan trades with a stop, a target and a reason. This first lesson is the foundation under all of it — the mechanics of why a price level can matter at all.

A chart is a record of decisions

Every candle on your chart is the footprint of an auction. Buyers and sellers meet, trade happens, and the price moves to wherever the two sides can agree. Most of the time that agreement drifts around without much drama. But at certain prices, something different happens: the market turns sharply, as if it hit something.

What it hit was a concentration of orders. Somewhere around that price, enough buyers (at a low) or sellers (at a high) were waiting that the side pushing price could not get through. The push ran out of fuel, the other side took over, and price reversed.

Here is the important part. Those orders do not all disappear when price leaves. Some were filled. Some were cancelled. But many participants were left with unfinished business at that price, and the market keeps a kind of memory of it.

Three groups with unfinished business

Think about who is left with an opinion after price turns sharply from a low. There are three groups, and each one gives the area a reason to matter again.

1. The buyers who got filled and want more. Someone bought heavily near the low and was rewarded. If price returns to the same area, the same logic that made them buy still applies — and now they have proof it worked. Many will buy again.

2. The buyers who missed it. Some traders saw the turn and hesitated. They watched price rally without them. If price comes back to the area, they get the second chance they have been hoping for, and they take it. This is the regret effect, and it is one of the most reliable forces on a chart.

3. The sellers who were caught. Traders who sold into the low watched the market turn against them. Many are still holding, hoping. If price comes back to where they sold, they finally get the chance to close at breakeven — and closing a short means buying. Their relief adds to the demand.

All three groups do the same thing when price returns: they buy. That is support. Flip every word and you have resistance: sellers who were rewarded, sellers who missed it, and trapped buyers looking for an exit, all selling when price comes back up to the area.

KEY POINT

A level matters because people are left with unfinished business there — orders to repeat, chances they missed, and losing positions they want to escape.

When price leaves in a hurry

The strongest memories are made when price leaves an area quickly. Think about why. If price drifted slowly through a level, everyone who wanted to trade there had time to do so. The business was finished. But if price exploded away from an area in a few large candles, a great many orders were never filled. Buyers who planned to buy there did not get the chance. The market left without them.

That makes the speed of departure one of the best clues you have about whether an area will matter again.

Compare that with an area price wandered through slowly, back and forth, for days. There is nothing unfinished there. Everyone who wanted to trade at that price had plenty of opportunity. When price returns to such an area, there is no particular reason for anything to happen — and usually nothing does.

Stop orders: the other half of the story

There is a second group of orders around every level, and beginners rarely think about them. When traders buy at support, most place their stop-loss a little below it. When traders sell at resistance, they place stops a little above it. So just beyond every obvious level sits a cluster of stop orders.

A stop order is a market order waiting to be triggered. A sell stop below support, once hit, sells at whatever price is available. That has two consequences you will study in detail later in the course:

  • Price is often drawn slightly through obvious levels. The stops beyond them are a pool of guaranteed orders, and larger traders who need to buy in size can use that burst of forced selling to fill their own orders. Price dips through the level, triggers the stops, then snaps back. This is the false break, and Lesson 7 is devoted to it.
  • When a level genuinely fails, the move accelerates. If there is no real buyer left behind support, the triggered stops feed on themselves and price falls quickly. Same trigger, opposite result. The difference is whether real interest was still waiting.

This is why we will never treat a level as a wall. A level is a neighbourhood where orders cluster, with fuel stored just outside it.

Every visit spends some of the memory

You will often hear that "the more times a level is tested, the stronger it becomes." Be careful with that. Every time price visits a support area, some of the waiting buy orders get filled. The ones that remain are fewer. Unless fresh buyers keep arriving, each visit leaves the area a little emptier than the last.

You can usually see this happening. The bounces get smaller. Price returns sooner. The reactions look tired.

That does not mean a level touched three times is useless. It means the character of the visits matters more than the count. A strong, sharp reaction on a fresh area is a very different thing from a fourth weary bounce. Lesson 4 turns this into a ranking system.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating a level as stronger simply because it has been touched many times. Repeated, weakening tests are often a sign the level is about to fail, not a reason to trust it more.

What this means for the rest of the course

Put these ideas together and you already have the logic of the whole method:

  • Look for areas price left quickly. That is where unfinished business lives.
  • Draw them as areas, not exact prices. Orders are spread across a range, and stops sit just beyond. Lesson 2 shows you exactly how.
  • Prefer fresh areas over tired ones. Each visit spends some of the memory.
  • Expect price to probe slightly beyond obvious levels. Stops are stored there, and they get used.
  • Never trade a level on faith. A level tells you where to pay attention. What price does when it gets there tells you whether to act.

That last point is the one that separates level traders who survive from those who don't. A support zone is a location, not a signal. Price arriving at support is not a reason to buy. Price arriving at support and then showing you that buyers are actually there — that is the beginning of a reason. The final module of this course is about exactly that evidence.

Going deeper

Experienced traders sometimes object that the "memory" explanation is too tidy. Orders get cancelled; the traders who bought at a low three months ago may have long since closed their positions; the order book you cannot see on a spot forex chart may look nothing like you imagine. All true. So why does the effect persist?

Partly because it is self-reinforcing. A level that is obvious on a daily chart is visible to everyone who looks at that chart. Enough participants expect a reaction there that they act on that expectation — placing buy orders, tightening stops, taking profit on shorts. The expectation produces the reaction. This is why visibility matters so much. A level that only you can see, found by zooming in and squinting, has no crowd behind it. A level that jumps off the chart has thousands.

It is also why higher timeframes carry more weight. A turn on a daily chart represents far more volume and far more participants than a turn on a five-minute chart. More participants means more unfinished business and more people watching. When a five-minute level and a daily level disagree, the daily level usually wins.

Two further caveats keep the idea honest:

Levels decay. A swing low from three years ago, in a completely different interest-rate regime, has fewer participants with any stake in it. Recent levels — and old levels that have recently been respected — usually matter more.

News overrides memory. A major data release or central-bank surprise can move price straight through any level without the usual reaction, because the new information changes what everyone thinks the currency is worth. Levels describe the market's memory of the past; they cannot protect you from new information. Many level traders simply stand aside around high-impact releases.

Finally, keep in mind what this course is and is not claiming. Support and resistance improves the location of your decisions: it tells you where the odds of a reaction are better than average and where your risk can be clearly defined. It does not tell you what will happen. Every example in this course comes with a stop for that reason. All charts here are illustrative training charts, built to show the concept clearly — real markets are messier, and you should expect that.

THE RULES
  • A level is a location, not a signal. Never act on price arriving at a level without evidence of a reaction.
  • Always treat levels as areas with stops clustered just beyond them.
  • Judge a level by the quality of past reactions and how quickly price left it, not by how many times it was touched.
  • Stand aside from level-based entries around high-impact news unless you have a separate, tested plan for it.

Summary

  • Levels exist because traders are left with unfinished business there: orders to repeat, missed chances to take, and losing positions to escape.
  • Areas that price left quickly hold the most unfilled orders and are most likely to matter again.
  • Stop orders cluster just beyond obvious levels, which explains both false breaks and fast genuine breaks.
  • Every visit spends some of the orders at a level; weakening bounces are a warning, not a strength.
  • A level tells you where to look. Price behaviour at the level tells you whether to act.

quiz.q: Why does price often react when it returns to an area where it previously turned sharply?
options: Because chart patterns repeat on a fixed cycle
Because traders are left with unfinished business there — unfilled orders, missed entries and trapped positions
Because brokers move price back to old levels
Because indicators are calibrated to old highs and lows
quiz.why: The memory of a level is made of people: those who want to repeat a successful trade, those who missed it, and those trapped on the wrong side who want to exit. The other options are not mechanisms that exist.

quiz.q: Trapped sellers who shorted right at a low that then rallied — what do they tend to do if price returns to their entry?
options: Sell more, adding to their position
Nothing — their stops were hit long ago
Close their short at breakeven, which means buying
Switch to a different currency pair
quiz.why: Many trapped traders hold and hope. When price returns to their entry they get out at breakeven, and closing a short is a buy order — adding to support.

quiz.q: Which area is most likely to hold a large amount of unfilled orders?
options: An area price drifted through slowly for several days
An area price left in a few large, fast candles
Any area that is a round number
The midpoint of yesterday's range
quiz.why: A fast departure means many traders who planned to trade there never got filled. A slow drift gives everyone time to finish their business.

quiz.q: In the 'every test spends some of the orders' chart, what was the warning sign before the zone broke?
options: The bounces were getting larger
The bounces were getting smaller and arriving sooner
Price touched the zone exactly four times
The zone was too wide
quiz.why: Shrinking bounces that return faster show defenders being used up. The count of touches alone is not the signal; the weakening character of the reactions is.

quiz.q: Where do stop-loss orders tend to cluster around an obvious support level?
options: Just above it
Exactly on it
Just below it
At the next resistance level
quiz.why: Traders who buy at support usually place stops a little below it. That cluster of sell stops sits just beyond the level and can fuel both false breaks and genuine breakdowns.

quiz.q: Price has just arrived at a strong daily support zone. According to this lesson, what should you do?
options: Buy immediately — strong support is a buy signal
Sell — it is about to break
Watch for evidence that buyers are actually present before considering a trade
Move the zone lower so it has more room
quiz.why: A level is a location, not a signal. Arrival tells you where to pay attention; the reaction you see there decides whether there is a trade.

lessons.title: Zones, Not Lines — Drawing Levels Honestly
lessons.summary: Build a support or resistance zone from wick to body at any swing point, size it sensibly, and stop mistaking normal wicks for broken levels.
lessons.html:
Most traders learn support and resistance by drawing a single horizontal line. It looks precise. It feels professional. And it quietly causes more bad decisions than almost anything else on a chart.

A thin line makes two promises no market can keep. It promises that the level sits at an exact price, to the pip. And it promises that a touch of that price means something, while a miss of three pips means nothing. Real markets do not work like that. As you saw in Lesson 1, a level is a cluster of orders spread across a range of prices, with stops sitting just beyond it. A cloud, not a laser.

This lesson replaces the line with a zone: a shaded band that says, honestly, "the interest lives somewhere in here." You will learn a repeatable way to build one from any swing point, how wide it should be, and how to read price once it is inside.

The line trader's problem

Here is a support level drawn the way most people draw it — a single line through the lows.

Three times price dipped through the line. Three times it closed back above and rallied. If you placed a stop a few pips under that line, you were taken out on every single test of a level that worked. If you treat a wick through the line as a break, you sold at the low three times.

The level did not fail. The drawing did. It was too precise for the thing it was trying to describe.

The same level, drawn as a zone

Now draw the same area as a band that runs from the bodies of the candles down to the bottom of the wicks.

Nothing about the price action changed. What changed is the question you ask. Instead of "did price touch the line?", you ask "did price close beyond the zone?" Inside the zone, wicks are expected; they are the visible sign of the level being defended. A candle that closes clearly beyond the far edge is a very different event, and Lesson 6 deals with it.

KEY POINT

Inside a zone, wicks are normal. What matters is where candles close.

Building a zone: the wick-to-body method

You need a repeatable way to draw zones, or they will expand and shrink to suit whatever you want to believe that day. Here is the method used throughout this course, described for support (turn it upside down for resistance).

  1. Find the turn. Go to the swing low — the candle, or small cluster of two or three candles, where the decline actually stopped and reversed.
  2. Mark the wick extreme. The lowest wick in that cluster is the far edge of the zone. It is the deepest point the market probed before buyers rejected it.
  3. Mark the body edge. Find the lowest candle body in the cluster — the lowest open or close. That is the near edge. It marks where the market refused to settle any lower.
  4. Shade between them. Wick extreme to body edge: that is your zone.

The logic is simple. Bodies show where the market accepted price; wicks show how far it probed before being rejected. The genuine interest lives between those two facts.

How wide is right?

Width is information, so do not shrink a zone just to make it look neater. A wide zone tells you the area was volatile and contested; you will need more room in your planning there. A tight zone tells you the turn was orderly and precise.

As rough guidance for major pairs:

  • Daily zones: commonly 20–60 pips tall.
  • 4-hour zones: commonly 10–30 pips.
  • 1-hour zones: commonly 6–20 pips.

A four-pip "daily zone" is a line with extra steps. A 150-pip "zone" is a region, and you cannot plan a trade around it. If your zone falls outside these ranges, look again — not because the numbers are rules, but because it usually means you have picked the wrong anchor candles.

When one wick is enormous

Sometimes the turn includes a single panic wick that stabs far beyond the others — a news spike, a thin market. Drawing the zone all the way to that wick produces something absurdly tall. In that case, draw the zone around where price actually turned and spent time, and mark the panic extreme separately as a reference line. You will use it later for stop placement, because a stop that sits inside a level's own panic range is a stop waiting to be hit.

COMMON MISTAKE

Drawing a zone exactly as wide as your stop-loss would like it to be. Draw the zone from the candles, then decide whether the trade is affordable. If it isn't, the answer is a smaller position or no trade, not a thinner zone.

Reading price inside the zone

Once you think in zones, three outcomes replace the line trader's single yes-or-no question:

  • Rejection. Price enters the zone, wicks into it, and closes back out on the side it came from. The level is being defended. This is the raw material for the rejection trades in Module 4.
  • Acceptance. Price closes inside the zone and keeps closing there. The battle is ongoing; nobody has won. You wait.
  • Break. Price closes clearly beyond the far edge — ideally with a strong candle and follow-through. The level has given way, and its role may now reverse (Lesson 5).

Notice that none of these is decided by a touch. They are decided by closes, and by what the candles look like.

Practice drill

A worked example, in numbers

Here is the method applied from start to finish (prices are for teaching only). EUR/USD on the 4-hour chart falls into a low and turns. The turn is made of three candles. The first is a red candle that opens at 1.0838 and closes at 1.0821, with a low of 1.0815. The second is a small candle that opens at 1.0821, wicks down to 1.0803 and closes at 1.0819. The third is a strong green candle that opens at 1.0819 and closes at 1.0846.

The wick extreme is the lowest low in the cluster: 1.0803. The body edge is the lowest open or close among the three candles: 1.0819. So the zone runs from 1.0803 to 1.0819 — 16 pips, comfortably within the normal range for a 4-hour zone.

Now suppose price returns two weeks later. A candle wicks to 1.0798 and closes at 1.0812. A line trader with a line at 1.0803 calls that a break. A zone trader notes a five-pip probe below the zone and a close back inside it, and starts watching for buyers. Same candle, very different decision — and only one of them is consistent with how the level was built.

Going deeper

Why body edge and not the close? The near edge uses the lowest body, which may be an open rather than a close. In a turn, the bullish candle that starts the rally often opens at the very spot the market stopped accepting lower prices. Using bodies, not just closes, captures that.

Clusters, not single candles. Swing points are often messy: two or three candles jostle at the low before price leaves. Use the whole cluster. The zone covers the extreme of any wick and the lowest body among the candles that formed the turn — not the candles of the decline into it, and not the rally out of it.

Zones from multiple touches. When a level has been tested several times, each test leaves its own wick-to-body band. Overlay them. The area where they overlap is the core of the zone; outlying wicks can be noted but need not stretch it. If the bands do not overlap at all, you may be looking at two separate levels, or at no level.

Spread and broker differences. Different brokers' charts show slightly different wicks, especially on lower timeframes and around the daily rollover. That is another reason zones beat lines: a three-pip difference in a wick should not change whether your level exists. If a level only "works" on one broker's feed, it isn't a level.

Zones and the volatility of the day. Average true range changes over time. A 30-pip daily zone drawn during a quiet summer may look thin when the pair is moving 150 pips a day. You do not need to redraw it, but your stops beyond it need to account for current volatility, which Lesson 9 covers.

THE RULES
  • Draw every level as a zone, from the extreme wick to the nearest body edge of the candles that formed the turn.
  • Judge a level by closes, not touches. A wick into or through a zone is not a break.
  • Never shrink a zone to make a stop fit. Size the position to the zone, or skip the trade.
  • Mark any panic-spike extreme separately; it matters for stop placement.

Summary

  • A single line promises a precision the market does not have, and leads to being stopped out or frozen by normal wicks.
  • Build zones from wick extreme to body edge at the candles that formed the turn.
  • Width tells you how contested the area is; on major pairs, daily zones are commonly 20–60 pips.
  • Trim a lone panic wick from the working zone but keep its extreme as a stop reference.
  • Inside a zone, read closes: rejection, acceptance or break.

quiz.q: Using the wick-to-body method on a swing low, where are the two edges of the zone?
options: The highest wick and the lowest wick
The lowest wick of the turn and the lowest candle body of the turn
The open of the first candle and the close of the last
The lowest close and a fixed 10 pips below it
quiz.why: The far edge is the deepest probe (the lowest wick); the near edge is where price refused to settle lower (the lowest body). Fixed-pip offsets ignore what the candles actually did.

quiz.q: Price wicks 12 pips below a support zone, then closes back inside it. What has happened?
options: The zone has broken; look for shorts
A rejection: price probed lower and was absorbed
Nothing — wicks are always meaningless
The zone needs redrawing 12 pips lower
quiz.why: Zones are judged on closes. A wick through and a close back inside is the level being defended, not broken. It is not meaningless either: it shows sellers being absorbed.

quiz.q: Your wick-to-body daily zone on EUR/USD is 55 pips tall, which makes your planned stop larger than you would like. What is the right response?
options: Redraw the zone at 20 pips so the stop fits
Use a smaller position size, or skip the trade if the plan does not work
Remove the stop altogether
Switch to a 1-minute chart and draw a tighter zone
quiz.why: Draw the zone from the evidence, then decide what is affordable. Shrinking the zone to suit the stop puts the stop inside the level's normal range.

quiz.q: A swing low contains one 50-pip news spike far below the other candles. How should it be handled?
options: Ignore the spike entirely
Extend the zone all the way down to the spike
Draw the working zone where the other candles turned, and mark the spike low as a reference for stops
Delete the level — spikes make levels unreliable
quiz.why: A lone panic wick makes the zone uselessly tall, but its extreme still matters: a stop placed inside that panic range is vulnerable.

quiz.q: In the drill chart, why did a line trader and a zone trader read the ringed candle differently?
options: They were looking at different timeframes
The line trader judged by touch; the zone trader judged by where the candle closed
The zone trader used an indicator
The line was drawn at a round number
quiz.why: The candle wicked through the line but closed inside the zone. Touch-based reading calls that a break; close-based reading calls it a rejection.

lessons.title: Finding Zones From Swing Points, Top Down
lessons.summary: Map the handful of zones that matter on a pair by working from the daily chart down to the 4-hour, using only clear swing points.
lessons.html:
You now know why levels exist and how to draw one honestly. The next question is the one that decides whether your charts help you or bury you: which levels do you draw?

Ask ten new traders to mark support and resistance on the same chart and you will get ten very different pictures. Most will be cluttered — a line at every wiggle, a zone at every pause, until the chart looks like a barcode. A cluttered chart feels thorough. In practice it is useless, because when every price is "at a level", none of them is.

This lesson gives you a routine. You will start on the daily chart, mark only swing points that anyone could see, refine them on the 4-hour, and finish with a clean map of three to seven zones that you can explain in one sentence each.

What a swing point is

A swing high is a peak with lower prices on both sides — a place where buyers ran out of steam and sellers took over. A swing low is the opposite: a trough where selling ran out and buying took over. Every zone in this course is built from one of these turns.

But not every bump on a chart is a swing worth marking. You are looking for turns that are obvious: price clearly travelled into the area, turned, and travelled clearly away. Here is the test used in this course:

  • Clear approach. Price moved into the turn with some purpose — not a sideways shuffle.
  • Clear departure. Price left the turn by a meaningful distance. As a guide, at least two or three times the height of an average candle on that timeframe, and preferably much more.
  • Visible without zooming. If you have to zoom in to see it, the rest of the market cannot see it either.
KEY POINT

Mark the turns where the market clearly changed direction. Ignore the pauses inside moves.

Why start on the daily chart

Lesson 1 explained that higher timeframes carry more weight: a daily turn represents far more participants, far more volume and far more unfinished business than a 15-minute turn. It is also seen by far more traders, which makes it self-reinforcing.

So the routine runs top down. You find the big levels first, because they are the ones most likely to stop price, and then use lower timeframes only to sharpen what you found. Working the other way — starting on the 15-minute chart and building up — produces dozens of minor zones, and you will never know which ones matter.

A practical hierarchy for a swing or day trader:

  • Weekly: one or two standing extremes — the levels that define the big picture. Glance at them; you rarely trade from them directly.
  • Daily: your main map. Three to seven zones within reach of current price.
  • 4-hour: refinement. Tighten daily zones and add any 4-hour zone that is clearly important inside a wide-open daily range.
  • 1-hour and below: execution only. You look here for entry triggers, not for new levels.

The routine, step by step

Step 1 — Set the window. On the daily chart, look at roughly the last six to twelve months. For a swing trader, that is the territory price can plausibly revisit. A level two thousand pips away is history, not analysis.

Step 2 — Squint. Lean back from the screen. Which highs and lows jump out? Those are your candidates. Write them down.

Step 3 — Draw wick-to-body zones at each candidate, using the method from Lesson 2.

Step 4 — Merge overlaps. If two candidate zones overlap or sit within a few pips of each other, they are the same level seen twice. Merge them into one zone.

Step 5 — Cull to the essentials. Keep zones within reach of current price — usually within one or two weeks' typical range — and drop any you could not justify in one sentence.

Refining on the 4-hour

Daily zones are often wide — 40, 50, 60 pips. That is honest, but it is a lot of room to plan a trade inside. The 4-hour chart helps you see where, inside that daily zone, the turn actually happened.

Switch to the 4-hour and look at the same area. Usually the daily turn shows up as a cluster of 4-hour candles with a clearer low. Draw a 4-hour wick-to-body zone around that cluster. It will sit inside, or overlap, the daily zone.

The daily zone tells you where to expect a reaction. The 4-hour refinement helps you plan how — where a trigger is most likely to appear and where a stop can go.

Two cautions. First, never let the refinement replace the daily zone. If price pushes through your 4-hour zone but is still inside the daily zone, the daily level has not failed. Second, do not refine below the 1-hour. Below that, you are no longer finding where the market turned; you are finding noise.

What a cluttered chart looks like

Here is the opposite of a working map.

The cluttered chart has a deeper problem than looking messy. It removes your ability to say no. When there is a level everywhere, you can always find one to justify the trade you already wanted. A clean chart forces patience: most of the time, price is in empty space, and the honest answer is "nothing to do yet".

COMMON MISTAKE

Drawing levels while you are itching to trade. Levels drawn in that mood have a habit of appearing exactly where you need them. Do your mapping at a set time — the weekend works well — and trade the map you drew when you were calm.

Keeping the map alive

A map is a working document. Three habits keep it honest:

Label every zone with its reason. A few words is enough: "D1 swing low, two turns, March." If you cannot write the label, delete the zone.

Update weekly, not hourly. Add new zones when a new obvious swing forms. Do not redraw old ones every time price comes near them.

Archive the dead. When a zone has been decisively broken and its retest (Lessons 5 and 6) has played out, or price has passed through it twice without any reaction, remove it. Old zones that no longer matter make you hesitate in clean territory.

Going deeper

How far back to look. The six-to-twelve-month window is a guide, not a rule. In a strong trend, price may have left old levels far behind; the relevant zones are the recent swing points within the trend. In a long range, levels from a year ago may still be live because price keeps returning to them. The question is always: could price plausibly reach this area within my holding period?

Weekly levels and daily zones that disagree. If a weekly extreme sits a little above a daily zone, treat the gap between them as contested territory. Price often stalls at the daily zone, then probes to the weekly level. Mark both; plan for both.

Swings that formed on news. A swing made by a single data-release spike is a weaker anchor than one built over several sessions. The spike may represent a few minutes of thin liquidity, not lasting interest. Keep such levels, but rank them lower (Lesson 4) and look for confirmation from later reactions.

The 'in-between' problem. On many charts there is a daily level, then 150 pips of open space, then another daily level. Traders get impatient in that space and start inventing 1-hour levels to trade. That is fine if you run a separate intraday method with its own rules. It is not fine to bolt minor levels onto a daily plan and treat them as equals. A 1-hour zone in the middle of a daily range is a lower-quality location, and your expectations — and position size — should reflect that.

Different traders, different maps. A scalper's "daily map" is a 1-hour map; a position trader's is weekly. The principle is identical — start one or two timeframes above where you execute, find the obvious turns, refine one step down. What changes is the scale.

THE RULES
  • Map top down: weekly glance, daily map, 4-hour refinement, 1-hour and below for execution only.
  • Only mark swing points with a clear approach and a clear departure, visible without zooming.
  • Keep three to seven zones within reach of current price. Merge overlaps; delete what you cannot justify in one sentence.
  • Draw and update the map at a set time, not while looking for a trade.

Summary

  • Zones are built only at obvious swing points: clear approach, clear departure, visible at a glance.
  • Start on the daily chart, because higher-timeframe turns carry more participants and more weight.
  • Refine daily zones on the 4-hour to plan entries and stops, but never let the refinement overrule the daily zone.
  • A clean map has three to seven zones and a lot of empty space. Clutter removes your ability to say no.
  • Label every zone with its reason, update weekly and archive dead zones.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best candidate for a zone?
options: A small pause halfway through a strong rally
A low where price fell steadily into the area, turned and rallied 150 pips
A level you found after zooming into the 5-minute chart
The opening price of every Monday
quiz.why: A clear approach and a clear departure make an obvious swing that the whole market can see. Pauses inside moves and zoom-only levels lack that visibility.

quiz.q: Why does this course map levels from the daily chart downwards?
options: Daily charts have fewer candles to look at
Higher-timeframe turns involve more participants and more unfinished business, so they matter more
Lower timeframes are not accurate
Brokers only show reliable data on the daily chart
quiz.why: A daily turn represents more volume and is seen by more traders, which makes it more likely to matter again. Lower timeframes are used to refine, not to discover.

quiz.q: Price has pushed through your 4-hour refinement zone but is still inside the wider daily zone. What does that tell you?
options: The daily level has failed
The refinement was wrong, but the daily level has not yet failed
You should immediately reverse your position
You should redraw the daily zone lower
quiz.why: The refinement is a planning aid. The daily zone is the level. It has not failed until price closes clearly beyond it.

quiz.q: In the cluttered-chart example, what is the deepest problem with eight zones in 120 pips?
options: The chart is hard to read on a phone
It removes your ability to say no — every price is 'at a level' and can justify a trade
It uses too much screen space
Zones should never be closer than 50 pips
quiz.why: When levels are everywhere, they stop being a filter. A clean chart forces you to wait for price to reach a meaningful location.

quiz.q: Two candidate zones on your daily chart overlap by most of their height. What should you do?
options: Keep both — overlap means double strength
Merge them into a single zone
Delete both
Keep only the higher one
quiz.why: Overlapping zones are the same level seen twice. Merge them so your map reflects one area of interest, not two.

quiz.q: When is the best time to draw and update your levels?
options: Whenever price gets close to a level
Right before entering a trade, to confirm it
At a set routine time, such as the weekend, when you are not looking for a trade
Every hour, to keep them accurate
quiz.why: Levels drawn while wanting a trade tend to appear wherever they are needed. A calm, routine mapping session keeps the map honest.

lessons.title: Ranking Zones — Which Levels Deserve Your Attention
lessons.summary: Score any zone on reaction strength, freshness, timeframe and confluence, so you know which levels to plan around and which to ignore.
lessons.html:
Your map now has a handful of honest zones. They are not equal. Some will stop price in its tracks; others will barely slow it down. If you treat them all the same — same attention, same position size, same confidence — you will spend your best patience on your worst levels.

This lesson gives you a simple scorecard. Four questions, each scored 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 8. It is not a magic formula and it does not predict anything. What it does is force you to look at each zone for the same reasons, in the same order, before price gets there and before you want the trade.

Factor 1: How strongly did price leave?

Lesson 1 explained that areas price left quickly hold the most unfinished business. This is the first and most important thing to judge.

  • 2 points: price left the zone in a sharp move — several large candles, little overlap, a clear distance travelled.
  • 1 point: a reasonable departure, but slower or choppier.
  • 0 points: price drifted away, overlapping and hesitant. There is little evidence of unfilled orders.

Factor 2: How fresh is it?

Every visit spends some of the orders at a zone. The first return to a zone usually gets the best reaction, because the unfilled orders are all still there.

  • 2 points: fresh — price has not returned to the zone since it formed.
  • 1 point: tested once, with a strong reaction.
  • 0 points: tested two or more times, or the last reactions were getting weaker.

Freshness is the factor most traders get backwards. "Tested many times" sounds strong. Usually it means the zone is running out of defenders. The exception is a zone that keeps producing strong, fast reactions on each visit — that suggests new interest arriving. Judge by the quality of the reactions, not the count.

Factor 3: What timeframe made it?

Higher-timeframe zones involve more participants, more volume and more attention.

  • 2 points: a weekly or daily zone.
  • 1 point: a 4-hour zone.
  • 0 points: a 1-hour zone or lower.

When a lower-timeframe zone gets in the way of a higher-timeframe one, the higher one usually wins.

Factor 4: What else lines up there?

Confluence means other independent reasons for orders to sit at the same price. The key word is independent. A 4-hour version of your daily zone is not confluence; it is the same zone again. Count only factors that would exist even if your zone didn't:

  • A round number inside the zone — 1.1000, 1.2500, 150.00. Traders and algorithms cluster orders, take-profits and stops at round prices. Whole figures (1.1000) matter more than half-figures (1.1050).
  • A role-reversal — the zone was previously the opposite type (old resistance now acting as support). Lesson 5 covers this.
  • Trend structure — the zone sits where a pullback would form a higher low in an uptrend, or a lower high in a downtrend.
  • A clear weekly extreme nearby.

Scoring:

  • 2 points: two or more independent factors.
  • 1 point: one factor.
  • 0 points: none.
KEY POINT

Confluence counts only independent reasons. The same zone seen on two timeframes is one reason, not two.

Putting the score together

Add the four factors for a total out of 8. Use it to decide how much attention a zone gets:

  • 6–8 — Prime zone. Plan for it in advance. Write down what you will look for and what you will do. These are the levels worth waiting days for.
  • 4–5 — Working zone. Tradeable with a clear trigger. Many of your trades will come from here.
  • 0–3 — Background zone. Keep it on the map as a possible target or obstacle, but do not trade from it.

Here is a worked example (illustrative only). A daily support zone on EUR/USD, formed by a sharp 180-pip rally (departure: 2). Price has not returned since (freshness: 2). It is a daily zone (timeframe: 2). The 1.0800 whole figure sits inside it, but there is no other confluence (confluence: 1). Total: 7 out of 8 — prime zone.

Compare a 4-hour zone (1) that price drifted away from (0), tested twice already (0), with nothing else nearby (0). Total: 1 out of 8 — background only. It might still turn price. You simply have no good reason to expect it to, and no reason to risk money on it.

COMMON MISTAKE

Scoring a zone after you want the trade. If you notice yourself hunting for a round number or a trend line to bump the score up, stop. Confluence gathered to justify a trade you already wanted is advocacy, not analysis.

Practice drill

Scores change — keep them current

A score is a snapshot, not a permanent rating. Three things change it, and your weekly mapping session (Lesson 3) is the time to update it:

  • A visit. When price returns to a zone, freshness drops. If the reaction was strong and fast, drop it by one point. If the reaction was weak, or price chopped around inside the zone, drop it to zero.
  • A break. A zone that has been decisively broken stops being scored in its original role. It may be re-scored in its new role as a possible flip (Lesson 5), starting from the strength of the break.
  • New confluence. A fresh weekly extreme forming nearby, or the trend structure shifting so that the zone now sits at a higher low, can add a point. Add it during the weekly review — not while price is approaching.

Here is how that plays out on one zone (illustrative). A 4-hour support scores 6 when first drawn: strong departure (2), fresh (2), 4-hour (1), sitting at a higher low in an uptrend (1). Price returns and bounces sharply: freshness drops to 1, total 5 — still a working zone. Price returns again and the bounce is half the size: freshness drops to 0, total 4 — borderline. A third visit with a feeble bounce would take it to background status before it ever breaks. The scorecard has quietly told you to stop trusting the level while it still looks intact.

Going deeper

Why a scorecard at all? Because your judgement in the moment is biased by whatever you saw last. If your previous trade lost at a zone, you will downgrade the next one; if it won, you will be too generous. A fixed scorecard written down beforehand is a way to make your Tuesday self agree with your Sunday self.

The weights are a starting point, not a law. This scorecard weights the four factors equally. Over months of journaling (the capstone covers this) you may find that, for the pairs and timeframes you trade, departure strength matters far more than confluence, or that freshness is decisive. Adjust the weights from your own records, not from anyone's opinion — including this course's.

Round numbers deserve nuance. Whole figures attract orders, but they also attract stops, which is why price often overshoots them by 10–20 pips before reacting. That makes a round number inside a zone a plus for the zone, but a liability for a stop placed right next to it. Lesson 9 returns to this.

Freshness and time. A fresh zone formed yesterday and a fresh zone formed eight months ago are both "untested", but the old one has fewer active participants with a stake in it. As a rough habit, treat a daily zone more than six to nine months old as one point lower on freshness unless something recent — a weekly extreme, a fresh flip — has re-energised it.

Do not double-count. Trend structure and role-reversal often coincide (old resistance becomes the higher-low area in an uptrend). That is fine — they are different reasons — but be honest that they describe related behaviour. If your score depends on counting every possible label for the same event, the zone is weaker than the number says.

Score is not signal. A prime zone tells you where to concentrate your attention and where your risk is best defined. It says nothing about whether price will react this time. The trigger rules in Module 4 still apply to every trade, and every trade still carries a stop.

THE RULES
  • Score every zone before price arrives: departure, freshness, timeframe, confluence — 0, 1 or 2 each.
  • Trade from prime (6–8) and working (4–5) zones only. Zones scoring 0–3 are targets and obstacles, not entries.
  • Count only independent confluence. The same zone on two timeframes is one factor.
  • Never raise a score after you have started wanting the trade.

Summary

  • Four factors rank a zone: how strongly price left, how fresh it is, what timeframe made it and what independent confluence it has.
  • Strong departures and fresh zones hold the most unfinished business. Repeated, weakening tests drain a zone.
  • Higher-timeframe zones usually beat lower-timeframe ones when they disagree.
  • Score 6–8 for prime zones, 4–5 for working zones, 0–3 for background zones you do not trade from.
  • A score tells you where to pay attention, never what price will do.

quiz.q: Which factor does this course treat as the best single clue that unfilled orders remain at a zone?
options: How many times it has been touched
How strongly and quickly price left it
Whether it is on a 1-hour chart
Whether it is drawn as a line
quiz.why: A fast, strong departure means many traders who wanted to trade there never got filled. Touch count tends to measure how much of the zone has been used up.

quiz.q: A daily zone was formed by a sharp rally, has never been revisited, and has the 1.2500 whole figure inside it — nothing else. What does it score?
quiz.why: Departure 2, freshness 2, timeframe 2, confluence 1 (one independent factor) = 7 out of 8.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as independent confluence for a daily support zone?
options: The same zone drawn on the 4-hour chart
A whole-figure round number inside the zone
The zone being shaded in a brighter colour
The fact that you want to buy there
quiz.why: A round number attracts orders for reasons unrelated to the zone. The 4-hour version of the same zone is the same evidence seen twice.

quiz.q: In the 'higher timeframe usually wins' chart, what happened?
options: Price turned at the 1-hour zone and never reached the daily zone
Price sliced through the 1-hour zone and turned at the daily zone
Both zones broke
The daily zone flipped to resistance
quiz.why: The minor 1-hour zone barely slowed the decline; the larger daily turn below held. Larger timeframes represent more participants.

quiz.q: A 4-hour zone scores 3 out of 8. How should you use it?
options: Trade from it with double size to compensate
Keep it as a possible target or obstacle, but do not trade from it
Delete it immediately
Add a round number to raise the score
quiz.why: Background zones are useful for planning targets and spotting obstacles, but there is no good reason to risk money entering from them.

quiz.q: You notice yourself searching for extra confluence on a zone because you want to take a trade there. What is the problem?
options: None — more confluence is always better
You are building a case for a decision already made, which inflates the score
Confluence should only be checked on weekends
Round numbers are not allowed in the score
quiz.why: Confluence found after you want the trade is advocacy, not analysis. Score zones before price arrives and before you have a stake in the answer.

lessons.title: Role Reversal — When Floors Become Ceilings
lessons.summary: Recognise when a broken zone is likely to switch roles, judge the quality of the flip, and spot the flips that fail.
lessons.module_title: Module 3 — How Price Behaves at Zones
lessons.html:
Here is one of the oldest and most useful behaviours on any chart. A support zone holds price up for weeks. Then it breaks. Price falls away — and some time later rallies back up to the old support. And there, where buyers used to defend, price turns down.

The floor has become a ceiling. Traders call this role reversal, or simply a flip. It works in both directions: broken resistance often becomes support, and broken support often becomes resistance.

Role reversal matters for two reasons. It gives you some of the cleanest trade locations available, because the level has already proved itself twice — once in each role. And it explains the "break and retest" pattern that the next lesson turns into a trade.

Why the flip happens

Go back to the three groups from Lesson 1 and watch what happens to them when support breaks.

The buyers who defended the zone. They bought at support. Now support has broken and they are sitting on losses. Many hold and hope. When price rallies back to the zone, they get the chance to close at breakeven — and closing a long means selling.

The traders who were waiting to sell. Some saw the break and wanted to sell, but did not want to chase price lower. A rally back to the broken zone is their second chance at a better price.

The traders who were right about the break. Those who sold the break are in profit. If price rallies back to the zone, many add to their position there, because it is the same logic that worked the first time.

All three groups do the same thing at the old support: they sell. The orders that made the zone a floor have been replaced by orders that make it a ceiling.

KEY POINT

When a zone breaks, the people who defended it become the people who will sell (or buy) it on the way back. That is why the zone often switches roles.

Resistance into support

The mirror image is just as common, and in an uptrend it is often the most useful zone on the chart.

In an uptrend, the old resistance often becomes the place where the next higher low forms. That is a natural point of confluence (Lesson 4): role reversal and trend structure in the same location.

What makes a high-quality flip

Not every broken zone flips. Before you treat a broken level as its new role, check four things.

1. The zone mattered before it broke. A flip borrows its strength from the original level. A zone that scored poorly in its first role will not suddenly become important in its second. Prime and working zones (Lesson 4) flip best.

2. The break was decisive. Look for at least one strong candle closing clearly beyond the zone, ideally followed by more candles moving away. A decisive break traps the defenders: they are now holding losses big enough to worry about. A break that oozes through the zone in small overlapping candles traps nobody.

3. Price travelled away before coming back. If price breaks the zone by five pips and immediately drifts back, the defenders never felt real pain. As a guide, look for price to have travelled at least the height of the zone again — preferably much more — before the retest.

4. It is the first retest. Just like a fresh zone in Lesson 4, the first return to a flipped zone usually gets the best reaction. Each retest after that spends some of the trapped orders.

The failed flip

Sometimes price breaks a zone, retests it from the other side, and instead of rejecting — it closes back through. The flip has failed. This is important information: the break was not real, and the original role of the zone is probably back in charge.

How do you know a flip has failed? The same way you know a zone has broken: by closes. One wick back into the zone means little. A candle that closes back on the original side of the zone — especially a strong one — says the break has been rejected. If you were short from the retest, your stop beyond the zone handles this for you. If you were waiting, the failed flip is a reason to stand aside or, for experienced traders, to look at the original role again.

COMMON MISTAKE

Treating every broken level as an automatic flip and selling the first touch from below. A flip has to be earned: a zone that mattered, a decisive break, real travel away and a first retest. Without those, you are trading a line on a chart, not a crowd of trapped traders.

From flip to trade

Recognising a flip is analysis. Trading one needs the same discipline as everything else in this course: a location, a trigger, a stop and a target. The next lesson builds that into a complete setup — the break-and-retest trade — but the outline is worth seeing now.

Suppose (illustratively) a daily support zone at 1.2440–1.2490 on GBP/USD has held three times. Price breaks it with a large daily close at 1.2385 and falls to 1.2280 over the next week — more than twice the zone's height away. That passes all four quality checks: the zone mattered, the break was decisive, price travelled, and the coming retest will be the first.

When price rallies back towards 1.2440, a flip trader does not simply sell at the zone edge. They wait for a bearish trigger at or inside the zone — evidence that sellers are defending it in its new role. The stop goes above the whole zone, at roughly 1.2500 or higher, not at 1.2445. The target is the next support on the map. If the distance to that target is not at least one and a half times the distance to the stop, there is no trade, however clean the flip looks.

Notice that everything in that plan can be written down before price arrives. That is the point. A flip is not something you discover in the heat of the moment; it is a scenario you prepared for when the zone broke.

Flips on different timeframes

Role reversal works on every timeframe, but its weight follows the same rule as everything else: higher timeframes carry more. A flipped daily zone can define a market's direction for weeks. A flipped 15-minute level might matter for an hour. When a lower-timeframe flip lines up with a higher-timeframe zone — for example, a 1-hour resistance flip sitting inside a daily resistance zone — treat the daily zone as the main event and the 1-hour flip as a refinement of it.

Going deeper

Flips and time. A flip is strongest when the retest comes reasonably soon after the break — within days on the 4-hour chart, within a few weeks on the daily. The trapped traders are still trapped and still watching. If the retest comes months later, many of them have already given up and closed at a loss somewhere else. The zone may still matter, but less.

The "polarity" of very large zones. Major daily or weekly zones can flip several times over months. Each flip weakens the next, for the same reason repeated tests weaken a zone. A level that has switched roles three or four times is often better treated as a magnet — somewhere price gravitates and chops — than as a clean turning point.

Flips inside ranges. In a sideways market, the middle of the range often contains a zone that has acted as both support and resistance many times. Those mid-range zones produce frequent, shallow reactions. They are useful for traders running a range method; they are poor locations for the trend-continuation trades in this course.

Overshoot on the retest. Retests frequently overshoot slightly into the zone, or even a little through it, before rejecting — the stops of traders who sold the break sit just above the zone and get used. This is why entries need a trigger (Module 4) rather than a limit order at the zone edge, and why the stop must sit beyond the whole zone, not at its near edge.

What the chart shows versus what we infer. We cannot see the trapped traders. We infer their existence from the price action: a zone that held, a break that was decisive, and a rejection on the return. That inference is useful because it is consistent with what the chart shows. It is still an inference, which is why every flip trade has a stop.

THE RULES
  • Treat a broken zone as a possible flip only if it mattered before, broke decisively on a close, and price travelled away before returning.
  • The first retest of a flipped zone is the one to plan for. Later retests carry less weight.
  • A close back through the zone on the original side means the flip has failed.
  • Never sell the first touch of a flipped zone (or buy it) without a trigger; retests often overshoot.

Summary

  • Broken support often becomes resistance, and broken resistance often becomes support, because trapped and waiting traders act at the old level.
  • Quality flips need a zone that mattered, a decisive close-through break, travel away, and a first retest.
  • Drifting, overlapping breaks trap nobody and rarely produce clean flips.
  • A close back through the zone on its original side means the flip has failed — useful information in itself.
  • Retests often overshoot into or slightly beyond the zone; plan stops beyond the whole zone.

quiz.q: Why does broken support often turn into resistance?
options: Because brokers reverse their orders at old levels
Because buyers trapped below their entries, and sellers who missed the break, both sell when price returns to the zone
Because indicators flip at that price
Because the zone gets thinner after a break
quiz.why: Trapped longs close at breakeven (selling), sellers who missed the break take their second chance, and those who sold the break add. All sell at the old support.

quiz.q: Which break is most likely to produce a clean flip?
options: Price oozes through the zone in small, overlapping candles
A strong candle closes well beyond the zone and price travels away before returning
A single wick pokes through and the candle closes back inside
Price breaks by two pips and returns immediately
quiz.why: A decisive close and travel away trap the zone's defenders in meaningful losses. That is the fuel for the flip.

quiz.q: Price broke below support, rallied back into the zone, and has now closed strongly back above it. What does that tell you?
options: The flip is confirmed; sell more
The flip has failed — the break has been rejected
Nothing; closes don't matter on retests
The zone should be redrawn lower
quiz.why: Flips, like breaks, are judged by closes. A strong close back on the original side says the break was not accepted.

quiz.q: In the 'resistance becomes support' chart, what additional confluence did the retest have?
options: A round number
It formed a higher low in a new uptrend
An RSI divergence
It was a weekly zone
quiz.why: After breaking out to a new high, the pullback to the old ceiling formed a higher low — role reversal and trend structure in the same place.

quiz.q: A zone has flipped from support to resistance and back again four times over several months. How should you treat it?
options: As a very strong level — it has proved itself many times
More as a magnet where price chops than as a clean turning point
As a zone with no meaning at all
As a weekly zone automatically
quiz.why: Each flip spends trapped orders. A level that keeps switching roles is often a place price gravitates to and chops around, not a clean reversal point.

lessons.title: Zone Breaks and the Retest Trade
lessons.summary: Tell a genuine break from a wick-through, trade the first retest of a broken zone with a defined stop and target, and know when to let a breakout go.
lessons.module_title: Module 3 — How Price Behaves at Zones
lessons.html:
Zones do not hold forever. Sooner or later every level on your map will break, and the way it breaks tells you a great deal about what comes next. A trader who cannot tell a genuine break from a probe will keep selling bottoms and buying tops. A trader who can will find that breaks produce some of the clearest trades on the chart — not on the break itself, but on the retest that often follows.

This lesson covers three things: how to judge whether a zone has really broken, how to trade the retest with a stop and target you can define in advance, and how to recognise the breakouts you should simply let go.

Wick through versus close through

Lesson 2 established the rule: zones are judged by closes, not touches. A break is no different. The question is never "did price go above resistance?" It is "did a candle close clearly above the zone — and did price keep going?"

A genuine break usually shows three things:

  1. A decisive close beyond the zone — not one pip beyond the edge, but a clear distance. As a rough guide on the 4-hour, at least a third of the zone's height, or more.
  2. A strong candle — a large body, small wick on the breakout side. The market is accepting the new prices, not probing them.
  3. Follow-through — the next candle or two continue in the same direction, or at least do not immediately reverse.

A break that closes just beyond the edge with a small body, then stalls, is at best uncertain. Treat it as unconfirmed. Lesson 7 covers what happens when it reverses.

KEY POINT

A break is a close, a strong body and follow-through. A wick beyond the zone is a probe until proven otherwise.

Why not just buy the breakout?

When price closes strongly above resistance, the obvious move is to buy straight away. Sometimes that works. Often it puts you in at a poor location: price has just travelled a long way, your stop has to go back below the zone (a long way away), and the market frequently pulls back before going further. You end up with a large stop, a modest target and a nervous few hours.

The retest solves this. After a genuine break, price often returns to the broken zone — now acting in its new role, as you saw in Lesson 5. If buyers defend it there, you get an entry close to the zone, a stop just beyond it, and the whole move to the next zone as your potential target.

The retest trade, step by step

Here is the method, described for a broken resistance (long). Turn it upside down for a broken support (short).

  1. Confirm the break. A strong close above the zone with follow-through, as described above.
  2. Wait for the return. Do nothing until price pulls back into or near the zone. No retest, no trade.
  3. Wait for a trigger in the zone. A bullish rejection candle — a pin bar, an engulfing candle, a strong close off the zone (Lesson 8 details these). The trigger is the evidence that buyers are actually defending the flipped level.
  4. Enter on the close of the trigger candle, or the open of the next.
  5. Stop below the whole zone, plus a buffer — not at the zone's near edge.
  6. Target the near edge of the next opposing zone on your map.
  7. Check the maths. If the distance to the target is less than about 1.5 times the distance to the stop, skip it.

Walk through the numbers (illustrative). Entry around 1.2784, stop at 1.2742 below the zone — 42 pips of risk. Target at 1.2850, just under the next resistance zone — 66 pips of potential reward. That is about 1.6R: acceptable, not spectacular. If you risk 1% of the account on the trade, the position size is set so that 42 pips equals 1%; the target, if reached, returns roughly 1.6%.

The retest that fails

Every method has losing trades, and this one loses in a specific way: price retests the zone, shows a trigger, and then breaks back through. When that happens, the stop beyond the zone does its job.

Look at what distinguishes the two charts after entry, because those clues are useful for management. In the winner, price left the zone immediately after the trigger. In the loser, price stalled just above the zone for several candles, unable to make progress. Hesitation after a trigger is not a reason to exit early on its own, but it is a reason not to add to the position and to expect that the stop may be tested.

COMMON MISTAKE

Moving the stop further away when a failing retest approaches it. The stop is beyond the zone for a reason: if price closes back through the zone, the break has failed and the trade idea no longer exists. Widening the stop turns a planned 1R loss into an unplanned larger one.

When there is no retest

Some breakouts never look back. Price breaks a zone and keeps going to the next one without ever returning. It is frustrating to watch, and it tempts you to chase.

You will miss moves like this. That is the price of a method that insists on good locations. Over many trades, the breakouts you miss cost you nothing; the breakouts you chase at poor prices cost you a great deal.

Practice drill

Managing the trade after entry

Once you are in, the plan does most of the work. Three rules keep you from undoing it:

  • Leave the stop beyond the zone until price has formed a new swing point clearly away from it. Only then consider tightening the stop to beyond that new swing.
  • Leave the target at the next zone. If price stalls short of it, that is the market's decision, not a reason to move the target closer in a panic or further away in hope.
  • Do not add to a trade that is hesitating. Price stalling just beyond the zone after a trigger is a warning sign, as the failed retest above shows.

Going deeper

Break timing and sessions. In forex, many decisive breaks happen at session opens — London and New York — when liquidity arrives. Breaks during the quiet Asian session on European pairs, or in the last hours of Friday, are more prone to reverse. This is not a rule, but it is a reason to give an Asian-session break less credit until it is confirmed.

Retest depth. Retests vary. Some only touch the near edge of the zone; some push all the way through it before rejecting. A retest that closes back inside the zone and then rejects is still valid. A retest that closes beyond the far edge is not a retest — it is a failed break, and the trade is off.

The second retest. If the first retest works and price later returns to the zone again, the second retest is weaker — the trapped orders have been partly spent. Some traders take it at reduced size; many skip it.

Entering without a trigger. A limit order at the zone edge gets better prices on the retests that work, and gets filled on every retest that fails. On balance, waiting for the trigger costs you some entries and some pips, and saves you from many of the failures. That trade-off is the core of this course's approach.

Expectancy, honestly. A hypothetical illustration of why the 1.5R minimum matters: if half your retest trades lose 1R and half win 1.6R, the average per trade is +0.3R before costs. If your winners only reach 1R, the same hit rate produces nothing after spreads. These numbers are invented to show the arithmetic, not a description of how any method performs. Your journal is the only place your real numbers come from.

THE RULES
  • A break needs a decisive close beyond the zone, a strong body and follow-through. A wick through is not a break.
  • Trade the first retest only, and only after a trigger candle in or at the zone.
  • Stop beyond the whole zone plus a buffer. Target the near edge of the next opposing zone.
  • Skip the trade if the target is less than about 1.5 times the risk.
  • No retest, no trade. Never chase a breakout with a stop back beyond the zone.

Summary

  • Breaks are confirmed by a decisive close, a strong body and follow-through, never by a wick.
  • The retest gives a better location than the breakout: entry near the zone, stop just beyond it, the move to the next zone as the target.
  • Wait for a trigger at the retest; enter, stop beyond the zone, target the next zone, and check the reward is at least about 1.5R.
  • Retests fail sometimes. The stop beyond the zone turns that into a controlled 1R loss.
  • When there is no retest, let the move go.

A large-bodied candle closing clearly above the zone, followed by more buying
A candle closing one pip above the zone edge
Price touching the zone three times
quiz.why: A genuine break is a decisive close, a strong body and follow-through. A wick is a probe; a one-pip close is unconfirmed.

options: Retests always succeed
The retest gives an entry close to the zone, a nearby stop and the move to the next zone as the target
Breakouts are not allowed in forex
Retests happen on every break

options: At the top edge of the broken zone
In the middle of the zone
Below the whole zone plus a buffer
At the high of the breakout candle
quiz.why: Retests often probe deep into the zone. Only a close back below the whole zone says the break has failed, so the stop belongs beyond it.

options: Take it — any trade with a stop is fine
Skip it — the reward (26 pips) is well under 1.5 times the risk (42 pips)
Move the stop to 1.2775 to improve the ratio
Ignore the next zone and target 1.2900

No retest, no trade — let it go
Sell, because it must come back
Buy with no stop
quiz.why: Chasing puts the stop far away for an unclear target. Missing some moves is the cost of insisting on good locations.
