Price stalled just above the zone for several candles, unable to make progress
The trigger candle was too large
The target was too close
quiz.why: Successful retests usually leave the zone quickly. Hesitation is not an exit signal on its own, but it warns that the stop may be tested.

lessons.title: False Breaks and Stop Runs
lessons.summary: Recognise when price has run the stops beyond a zone and been rejected, trade the reclaim with a defined stop, and tell it apart from a break that is real.
lessons.module_title: Module 3 — How Price Behaves at Zones
lessons.html:
You have probably lived this. You buy at support. You put your stop a few pips below it, like everyone tells you to. Price dips, takes your stop by four pips — and then rallies 150 pips without you. It feels personal. It feels like someone saw your order.

Nobody saw your order. But plenty of people could see where orders like yours were likely to be, because they were sitting just below an obvious level, exactly where the textbooks put them. This lesson explains the stop run, also called a false break or fakeout: what it is, why it happens at obvious levels, how to read it as it forms, and how to turn it from something that happens to you into a setup you can trade with a defined risk.

Where the stops are

Recall Lesson 1. Traders who buy at support place sell stops just below it. Traders who sell at resistance place buy stops just above it. The more obvious the level, the larger the cluster. And stops are market orders waiting to be triggered: when price reaches them, they execute at whatever price is available.

That makes the area just beyond an obvious zone a pool of guaranteed orders. For a large participant who wants to buy a lot without pushing the price up against themselves, a burst of forced selling from triggered stops is useful: it supplies sellers to buy from. Whether anyone is doing this deliberately in a given case is unknowable from your chart. What you can see is the footprint — and it is distinctive.

The anatomy of a false break

A false break at support has a recognisable shape:

  1. An obvious zone. Several clear reactions, visible to everyone. That is what puts the stops there.
  2. A push beyond the zone. Either a long wick through it (the version you met in Lesson 2), or — more deceptively — a candle that actually closes beyond it.
  3. A fast, strong reclaim. Within one to three candles, price closes back inside or above the zone, usually with a large body. This is the critical part. The market tried lower prices, triggered the stops, and found more buyers than sellers.
  4. Trapped breakout traders. Anyone who sold the break is now underwater with their stop above. As price rises, their buy stops add fuel.

The reclaim is what separates a false break from a genuine one. A genuine break, as you saw in Lesson 6, closes beyond the zone and keeps going. A false break closes beyond it and is dragged back.

KEY POINT

A false break is defined by the reclaim: a fast, strong close back inside the zone. Without that, you are looking at a break.

Trading the reclaim

Here is the setup, described for support (reverse it for resistance).

  1. The zone must be worth trading. A working or prime zone from Lesson 4, ideally with obvious prior reactions.
  2. Price pushes beyond the zone — a wick or a close.
  3. Wait for the reclaim candle: a strong close back inside the zone, within three candles of the push. A strong close means a large body finishing in the upper part of its range.
  4. Enter on the close of the reclaim candle, or the open of the next.
  5. Stop below the spike low, plus a buffer. The spike low is now the line in the sand: if price goes back below it, the stops have been run and there were no buyers waiting after all.
  6. Target the near edge of the next resistance zone. Check the reward is at least about 1.5 times the risk.

The numbers (illustrative): entry 1.2676, stop 1.2612 (64 pips of risk), target 1.2772 (96 pips) — 1.5R. Notice that the stop is wider than for a normal rejection trade, because it must sit beyond the spike, not just beyond the zone. That is the cost of this setup. If the stop makes the reward less than about 1.5R, skip it, however good the reclaim looks.

When the "false break" is real

Not every push beyond a zone comes back with conviction. Sometimes price reclaims weakly — a small candle that closes barely inside the zone — and then rolls over again. A trader who calls every break "a stop run" will buy that weak reclaim and lose.

Compare the two reclaims:

  • Strong: a large body, closing well inside or above the zone, ideally engulfing the breakdown candle. The next candle does not immediately give it back.
  • Weak: a small body, closing barely inside the zone, often with a long upper wick. The candles after it hesitate.

A weak reclaim is not a setup. It is a pause in a breakdown. The disciplined response is to skip it — and the trade on the chart above should not have been taken under this lesson's rules. It is shown because almost every trader takes this trade at some point, and the stop below the spike is what keeps the mistake small.

COMMON MISTAKE

Labelling every break a "stop hunt" after the fact. The story is always available in hindsight. Before the fact, the only evidence that counts is a strong, fast reclaim. No reclaim, no false break.

False breaks at round numbers

Round numbers attract stops in huge numbers, because traders love to put orders at or just beyond them. That makes zones containing a whole figure especially prone to overshoots.

Look again at the caption. This false break was clean, and it worked — but the reward was only about 1.3R once the stop sat properly above the spike. Under this course's rules, it is a skip. Good-looking setups with poor arithmetic are still poor trades. Do not let a result you can see in hindsight change the rules you apply in advance.

Reading the push in real time

When price pushes beyond a zone you are watching, you do not know yet whether it is a break or a stop run. Ask these questions in order, candle by candle:

  1. Did the candle close beyond the zone, or only wick? A wick-only push is a candidate pin bar. A close beyond is a candidate break — or a candidate two-candle false break.
  2. How did the next candle behave? Follow-through away from the zone points to a break. A strong move back towards the zone points to a stop run.
  3. Has a candle closed back inside, strongly? Only now, with a strong reclaim, is there a false-break setup.
  4. Does the arithmetic work? Stop beyond the spike, target at the next zone, at least 1.5R.

Until question 3 has a clear yes, you have no trade in either direction. Patience here is not passivity; it is waiting for the market to tell you which of two stories is true.

Going deeper

Wick-only versus close-beyond false breaks. A wick through the zone with a close back inside (a pin bar) is a false break in miniature, completed within one candle. The two-candle version — close beyond, then reclaim — traps more traders, because breakout traders acted on the close. That can produce sharper reversals, but also requires a wider stop. Neither is better in principle; the arithmetic decides.

How far beyond is too far? A stop run that travels a long way beyond the zone — say, more than the zone's own height again — starts to look less like a run on nearby stops and more like a genuine move that happened to reverse. The reversal can still be traded, but the stop gets so wide that the trade rarely passes the 1.5R test.

The second attempt. After a failed false break (the weak reclaim above), price often retests the zone from below as new resistance — Lesson 5's flip. The trader who lost on the weak reclaim can, with discipline, find a valid short on that retest. The zone did not stop mattering; it changed role.

Higher-timeframe context. False breaks against the higher-timeframe trend are more likely to fail. A stop run below support in a strong daily downtrend is often just the first leg of the breakdown. A stop run below support that forms a higher low in a daily uptrend has the bigger picture on its side.

Language discipline. Phrases like "smart money hunted the stops" describe an interpretation. The chart shows a push beyond a level, a burst of activity, and a reclaim. That is enough to trade. Price first, story second — and never let the story talk you into a trade the price action has not confirmed.

THE RULES
  • Only trade false breaks at working or prime zones with obvious prior reactions.
  • The reclaim must be strong and fast: a large-bodied close back inside the zone within three candles.
  • Stop beyond the spike extreme plus a buffer, not just beyond the zone.
  • Target the next opposing zone. If the reward is less than about 1.5 times the risk, skip it.
  • A weak reclaim is a pause in a breakdown, not a setup.

Summary

  • Stops cluster just beyond obvious zones, especially near round numbers. Pushes into those clusters are common.
  • A false break is a push beyond the zone followed by a fast, strong reclaim. The reclaim defines it.
  • Trade it on the reclaim close, with the stop beyond the spike and the target at the next zone — if the arithmetic works.
  • Weak reclaims often fail. Skip them.
  • The story of who hunted whose stops is optional. The price action is not.

quiz.q: Why do false breaks happen most often at obvious levels?
options: Because obvious levels are always wrong
Because obvious levels have the largest clusters of stop orders just beyond them
Because brokers move prices at obvious levels
Because indicators lag at obvious levels
quiz.why: The more obvious the level, the more traders place stops just beyond it. That pool of resting orders is what pushes into and through the zone tend to use.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of a false break, as opposed to a genuine break?
options: A long wick
A fast, strong close back inside the zone after the push beyond it
A round number nearby
High volatility
quiz.why: Genuine breaks close beyond and keep going. False breaks close beyond (or wick beyond) and are reclaimed strongly and quickly.

quiz.q: In a false-break long, where does the stop belong?
options: Just below the zone
Below the spike low, plus a buffer
At the entry price
At the midpoint of the reclaim candle
quiz.why: The spike low is the line in the sand. If price returns below it, the push was not a stop run with buyers behind it.

quiz.q: A candle closes below support, and the next candle closes just 2 pips back inside the zone with a small body and a long upper wick. What does this lesson say?
options: Strong reclaim — buy
Weak reclaim — not a setup
Genuine break — sell immediately with no stop
Redraw the zone lower
quiz.why: A small body barely back inside, with selling into it, shows buyers are not in control. Weak reclaims often fail.

quiz.q: A clean false break above 150.00 offers entry 149.84, stop 150.38 and the next support at 149.14. Should you take it under this course's rules?
options: Yes — it is a clean false break at a round number
No — 70 pips of reward for 54 pips of risk is about 1.3R, under the 1.5R minimum
Yes, but move the stop to 150.10 to improve the ratio
Only if the RSI agrees
quiz.why: Good-looking setups with poor arithmetic are still poor trades. Tightening the stop inside the spike just makes it more likely to be hit.

quiz.q: Which statement keeps the right discipline about 'stop hunts'?
options: Large players always hunt retail stops, so fade every break
The chart shows a push beyond a level and a reclaim; that observable behaviour, not the story, is what you trade
Stop hunts can be predicted from the economic calendar
Never use stops, so they can't be hunted
quiz.why: Intent is an interpretation. Price action is the evidence. Removing stops turns a controlled loss into an uncontrolled one.

lessons.title: Trading Rejections — Candle Triggers at the Zone
lessons.summary: Use three precise candle triggers to decide when a zone is being defended, and know when the right candle in the wrong place is no trade at all.
lessons.html:
Everything so far has been about location: where the zones are, how good they are, how they break and flip. Location tells you where to pay attention. It does not tell you when to act.

Price arriving at a support zone is not a reason to buy. The zone might hold; it might break; it might be run for stops first. What you need is evidence, visible on the chart, that the other side has actually turned up and is defending the level. In this course that evidence is a trigger candle — one of three specific candle patterns that show rejection, closing in or at the zone.

This lesson defines those three triggers precisely, shows how to turn them into entries with stops and targets, and spends as much time on when not to act as on when to act.

Why candles, and why at the zone

A single candle is a compressed story of one period's battle. Its open, high, low and close tell you who pushed, how far, and who won by the end. Most candles, most of the time, tell you very little. But at a zone that you scored and planned for in advance, a candle that shows rejection carries real information: the level was tested, and it pushed back.

Notice the order. Zone first, candle second. A perfect-looking pin bar in the middle of nowhere is just a candle with a long wick. The same candle at a prime support zone is a trigger. The zone gives the candle its meaning.

KEY POINT

The zone is the reason. The candle is the evidence. You need both.

Trigger 1: the pin bar

A bullish pin bar at support has a long lower wick, a small body, and closes in the upper part of its range. It says: sellers pushed price down into the zone, buyers took it all back before the close.

The definition used in this course (reverse it for a bearish pin at resistance):

  • The lower wick is at least twice the length of the body.
  • The candle closes in the upper third of its full range.
  • The wick reaches into the zone (or through it), and the candle closes back inside or above the zone.
  • The candle is noticeably larger than the few before it. A tiny pin in a quiet market says little.

Trigger 2: the engulfing candle

A bearish engulfing candle at resistance opens at or above the previous candle's close and closes below the previous candle's open, swallowing its whole body. It says: buyers pushed into the zone, and in the next period sellers not only stopped them but reversed the entire previous candle.

The definition used in this course (reverse it for bullish engulfing at support):

  • The previous candle is bullish and pushes into or through the resistance zone.
  • The engulfing candle's body completely covers the previous candle's body.
  • It closes back below the zone, or at least in the lower part of it.
  • It closes in the lower third of its own range — sellers kept control into the close.

Trigger 3: the reclaim close

You met the third trigger in Lesson 7. Price pushes beyond the zone — a close through it — and then a strong candle closes back inside within one to three candles. It is the two-candle cousin of the pin bar, and it carries the same message: the push beyond the zone was rejected.

Use the same quality test as Lesson 7: a large body, a close well back inside the zone, and ideally a close above the breakdown candle's open. Stops go beyond the spike extreme, which often makes this the widest-stop trigger of the three.

Entries, stops and targets

For all three triggers, the mechanics are the same:

  • Entry: on the close of the trigger candle, or at the open of the next candle. Some traders wait for the next candle to move in their direction first, accepting a slightly worse price for extra confirmation. Choose one approach and use it consistently.
  • Stop: beyond the trigger's extreme and beyond the zone, plus a buffer. Lesson 9 covers buffers in detail.
  • Target: the near edge of the next opposing zone on your map.
  • Size: set so that the distance from entry to stop equals your fixed risk per trade — for example 0.5–1% of the account (illustrative).

The right candle in the wrong place

Here is the trap that catches traders who learn candle patterns before they learn location.

A pin bar here is just a candle with a long wick. There is no zone behind it, no trapped traders, no unfinished business. And practically, there is nowhere sensible for a stop. Below the wick? That is an arbitrary price. Below the next support? That is 70 pips away. Either way you are trading a pattern, not a level.

COMMON MISTAKE

Learning candle patterns first and hunting for them everywhere. A trigger only counts in a zone you scored before price arrived. Everywhere else, it is noise with a name.

A good trade that lost

The final chart matters as much as any other in this course. It shows a trade that met every rule — prime zone, clean trigger, correct stop, sound target — and lost.

There is nothing to fix in this trade. The zone was real, the trigger was valid, the risk was defined before entry and the stop was where the trade idea became wrong. Sometimes the zone simply fails. If you change your rules every time a valid trade loses, you will end up with no rules — just a collection of reactions to your most recent loss.

The useful questions after a loss like this are about process, not outcome: was the zone scored before price arrived? Was the trigger within definition? Was the stop placed where the idea was invalidated, and the position sized to it? If yes to all, the loss is the cost of doing business. Record it and move on.

Practice drill

Going deeper

Why fixed definitions? Candle patterns are notoriously elastic: given enough wanting, almost any candle can be called a pin bar. A written definition — wick twice the body, close in the upper third, wick into the zone — is a guard against your own enthusiasm. You can tighten or loosen the numbers from your journal later, but use some numbers.

Trigger timeframe. Use the timeframe one step below your map for triggers: a daily zone with a 4-hour trigger, a 4-hour zone with a 1-hour trigger. Triggers on the same timeframe as the zone come late and need wide stops; triggers far below it (a 5-minute pin bar at a daily zone) appear constantly and mean little.

Confirmation entries. Waiting for the candle after the trigger to break the trigger's high (for longs) filters out some failures and costs you some entry price and some trades that run without you. Neither choice is right in general; the journal tells you which suits you.

Size of the trigger relative to the zone. A pin bar whose wick is three times the height of the zone, on a quiet day, is unusual and powerful. A pin bar smaller than the zone is weaker evidence — it is just jostling inside the level. Context and proportion matter more than shape alone.

News candles. A huge pin bar formed during a data release reflects a few minutes of thin, jumpy liquidity. It can work, but it is a less reliable signal of sustained defence than a pin formed during normal trading. Many traders simply ignore triggers formed on major news.

Outcome thinking. In any random sequence of valid trades, losing streaks of five or six in a row are normal even for methods that are profitable over time. Fixed risk per trade (for example 0.5–1%) exists so that such a streak is an unpleasant week, not the end of an account.

THE RULES
  • No zone, no trade. Triggers only count inside a zone scored before price arrived.
  • Use only the three defined triggers: pin bar, engulfing candle, strong reclaim close.
  • Stop beyond the trigger extreme and the zone, plus a buffer. Target the next opposing zone.
  • Judge losing trades by process, not outcome. Do not change the rules after a single valid loss.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • The zone is on my map, scored 4 or more before price arrived
  • A trigger has closed: pin bar, engulfing, or strong reclaim, within definition
  • The stop sits beyond the trigger extreme and the whole zone, plus a buffer
  • The target is the near edge of the next opposing zone, and the reward is at least 1.5R
  • Position size is set so the stop distance equals my fixed risk per trade
  • No high-impact news is due before the trade has had time to work

Summary

  • A zone tells you where; a trigger candle tells you when. You need both.
  • The three triggers are the pin bar, the engulfing candle and the strong reclaim close, each with a written definition.
  • Enter on the trigger close, stop beyond the trigger and the zone, target the next opposing zone, size to a fixed risk.
  • The right candle in the wrong place is no trade.
  • Valid trades lose. Judge them on process.

quiz.q: Which candle meets this course's definition of a bullish pin bar at support?
options: Lower wick 6 pips, body 10 pips, closes mid-range
Lower wick 22 pips, body 6 pips, closes in the top fifth, wick into the zone
Upper wick 20 pips, body 5 pips, closes near the low
No wicks, large green body
quiz.why: A pin bar needs a lower wick at least twice the body, a close in the upper third and a wick reaching into the zone.

quiz.q: What makes a bearish engulfing candle at resistance a valid trigger?
options: It is red
Its body covers the previous bullish candle's body and it closes in its lower third, back below or low in the zone
It has a long upper wick
It forms anywhere in an uptrend
quiz.why: Engulfing means reversing the whole previous body and finishing with sellers in control, at the zone.

quiz.q: A perfect pin bar forms 70 pips above the nearest support zone. What should you do?
options: Buy — the pattern is perfect
Nothing — there is no zone, so it is not a trigger
Buy with a stop at the support zone 70 pips away
Sell, because pin bars fail away from zones
quiz.why: Zone first, candle second. Without a level behind it, the pin has no meaning under this method and no sensible stop.

quiz.q: In the 'every rule followed' chart, what is the right conclusion?
options: Engulfing candles do not work on USD/JPY
The stop should have been wider
The process was correct; this was a normal 1R loss
Support zones should be scored higher before trading
quiz.why: Zone, trigger, stop and target were all valid. Some valid trades lose; changing rules after one loss destroys consistency.

quiz.q: Your map is on the daily chart. On which timeframe does the lesson suggest looking for triggers?
options: Weekly
Daily
4-hour
1-minute
quiz.why: One step below the map. Same-timeframe triggers come late with wide stops; far lower timeframes produce frequent, meaningless triggers.

quiz.q: In the drill, why was there no trigger?
options: The zone score was too low to trade
None of the candles closed in its upper third or engulfed the previous candle; the last closed at the zone's bottom
There were too many wicks
It was the wrong time of day
quiz.why: Small wicks show some absorption, but no candle showed buyers winning by the close. Waiting was correct.

lessons.title: Stops Beyond Zones, Targets to the Next Zone
lessons.summary: Place stops where the trade idea is genuinely wrong, set targets from your zone map, size positions from the stop, and reject trades that lack room.
lessons.html:
Two traders take the same trade from the same zone with the same trigger. One puts the stop ten pips under the entry because it "feels about right" and aims for "around 2R". The other puts the stop beyond the zone, where the idea is wrong, and aims for the next zone on the map, where the next crowd of orders sits. Over a hundred trades, these two will have very different results, and the difference has nothing to do with entries.

This lesson is about the parts of a trade that most courses rush: where the stop goes, where the target goes, how big the position is, and when the honest answer is "this trade does not fit". Support and resistance is unusually good at answering all four, because the zones themselves tell you where the trade is wrong and where it is likely to run out of road.

Where the trade is wrong

A stop-loss is not a pain threshold. It is the price at which the reason for the trade no longer exists.

For a long from support, the reason is "buyers are defending this zone". When is that reason gone? Not when price wicks into the zone — wicks into the zone are the zone being tested, which is what you expected. The reason is gone when price trades beyond the whole zone and beyond the trigger's extreme, by enough to rule out ordinary noise.

So the stop goes:

  1. Beyond the far edge of the zone,
  2. Beyond the extreme of the trigger (the pin's wick, the engulfing candle's low, the reclaim's spike),
  3. Plus a buffer for spread and noise.

Whichever of the first two is further away sets the base; the buffer goes on top.

Look at the arithmetic in that caption. The tight stop looked better: 3.6R instead of 1.6R. But the tight stop was inside the zone, inside the range where price was always likely to wander. A 3.6R trade that gets stopped out by normal behaviour is worth less than a 1.6R trade that has room to work.

KEY POINT

A stop belongs where the trade idea is wrong — beyond the zone and the trigger — not where the loss feels comfortable.

How big a buffer?

The buffer exists because wicks overshoot, spreads widen and every broker's feed differs slightly. A workable starting point for major pairs:

  • 1-hour trades: 3–6 pips beyond the zone/trigger.
  • 4-hour trades: 5–10 pips.
  • Daily trades: 10–20 pips.

Scale up for more volatile pairs (GBP crosses, gold) and for unusually volatile weeks. A slightly better rule of thumb, once you are comfortable: around 10–15% of the pair's average daily range on the trade timeframe. The exact figure matters less than using the same logic every time.

Round numbers and stops

Round numbers attract stops, and stop clusters attract price (Lesson 7). So the worst place for your stop is exactly on a round number or a few pips beyond it, where everyone else's is.

When a zone sits on or next to a round number, push the stop clearly past the figure — 10 pips or more beyond it on an hourly or 4-hour trade. Yes, that increases your risk in pips. Position sizing takes care of that.

Targets: the next zone

Your zone map is also your target map. A long from support has a natural destination: the near edge of the next resistance zone above. That is where the next crowd of sellers sits, where the trade is most likely to stall.

Three rules keep targets honest:

  1. Target the near edge, not the middle or the far edge. Price often reacts as soon as it touches the zone. Aiming for the far edge asks the market to push through a crowd of opposing orders to reward you.
  2. Use the next zone that scored 4 or more. Background zones (0–3) may slow price, but they are not where you expect it to stop. Note them as possible obstacles.
  3. Do not invent targets. If there is no clear zone above, use a conservative fixed multiple — 2R is a common choice — rather than a hopeful one.

Position size comes from the stop

Once the stop is set by the chart, the position size follows from the risk you have chosen, not the other way round.

Position size = (account × risk per trade) ÷ (stop distance in pips × pip value).

An illustrative example: a £10,000 account risking 1% per trade risks £100. If the stop is 40 pips away and one standard lot on EUR/USD is worth about £8 per pip (the exact value depends on the exchange rate), then the position is £100 ÷ (40 × £8) ≈ 0.31 lots. If the stop were 20 pips away, the same £100 would allow about 0.62 lots.

This is why you never need to squeeze a stop into a zone. A wider stop simply means a smaller position. The pounds at risk stay the same.

When there is no room

The last check before any trade is whether the distance to the target justifies the distance to the stop. This course uses 1.5R as a minimum: the reward to the target must be at least one and a half times the risk to the stop.

This filter costs you trades, and some of the trades it removes would have won. It also stops you taking large numbers of trades where a winner barely pays for a loser. Over time, that matters more.

COMMON MISTAKE

Fixing a poor ratio by moving the stop closer or the target further away. Either change replaces the chart's answer with your preferred one. The stop and target come from the map; the ratio is simply what they produce.

Practice drill

Putting it together

A complete example (illustrative): a short from a resistance zone at 1.0880–1.0900 on EUR/USD after a bearish engulfing candle with a high of 1.0904 that closes at 1.0872. The stop goes above the higher of the zone's ceiling (1.0900) and the trigger's high (1.0904), plus an 8-pip buffer: 1.0912, which is 40 pips of risk. The next support zone on the map runs from 1.0790 to 1.0810, so the target is just above its near edge, at 1.0812: 60 pips of reward, 1.5R — right on the minimum. With 1% of a £10,000 account at risk (£100) and roughly £8 per pip per standard lot, the position is about 0.31 lots. Every number came from the chart or the risk rule. None came from a feeling.

Going deeper

Moving stops to breakeven. A common habit is to move the stop to entry once the trade is 1R in profit. It feels safe. With zone-based trades it often converts winners into breakeven exits, because price frequently revisits the zone edge after leaving it. A more defensible rule: only tighten the stop to a new structural point — beyond a new higher low that has formed above the zone. If no such point exists yet, leave the stop where the original idea is invalidated.

Partial profits. Taking part of the position off at an intermediate background zone and the rest at the main target is reasonable, provided you decide it in advance and calculate the blended R honestly. Splitting a 1.6R trade into half at 0.8R and half at 1.6R produces a 1.2R trade when both hit — which, by this course's filter, you would not have taken in the first place.

Spread and costs. On short-timeframe trades, the spread can be a meaningful fraction of the stop. A 2-pip spread on a 15-pip stop is a 13% hidden cost on every trade. Include the spread in your R calculation, especially for 1-hour trades and less liquid pairs.

When the stop distance is extreme. If a zone is so wide, or a trigger so long, that the stop needs to be three or four times your usual distance, the position size becomes very small and the trade is fine mathematically. But extreme stops often coincide with extreme conditions — news, illiquid sessions. It is reasonable to have a maximum stop distance per timeframe and simply skip trades beyond it.

Expectancy, illustrated. A hypothetical method that wins 45% of the time at an average of 1.8R and loses 55% at 1R produces 0.45 × 1.8 − 0.55 × 1 = +0.26R per trade before costs. Drop the average winner to 1.2R and it becomes −0.01R. These numbers are invented to show why the 1.5R filter exists; they are not a description of what this or any method achieves.

THE RULES
  • Stop beyond the far edge of the zone and the trigger's extreme, plus a buffer. Never inside the zone.
  • Keep stops clear of round numbers by a meaningful margin.
  • Target the near edge of the next opposing zone that scores 4 or more.
  • Size the position from the stop and a fixed risk per trade (for example 0.5–1%, illustrative).
  • Minimum 1.5R to the target. Never move the stop or target to make a trade pass.

Summary

  • The stop goes where the trade idea is wrong: beyond the whole zone and the trigger's extreme, plus a buffer.
  • Tight stops inside the zone produce attractive ratios and frequent avoidable losses.
  • Keep stops away from round numbers, where crowded stops attract overshoots.
  • The next opposing zone's near edge is the target. Your map is your target map.
  • Position size comes from the stop and a fixed risk. If the trade cannot offer about 1.5R, skip it.

quiz.q: For a long from a support zone after a pin bar, where does the stop belong?
options: Halfway into the zone
Beyond the zone's far edge and the pin's wick, plus a buffer
At a fixed 10 pips below entry
At the previous day's low regardless of the zone
quiz.why: The trade idea is wrong only when price moves beyond the whole zone and the trigger's extreme. A buffer handles noise and spread.

quiz.q: A tight stop inside the zone gives 3.6R; a stop beyond the zone gives 1.6R. Which is better, and why?
options: 3.6R — a bigger ratio always wins
1.6R — the tight stop sits where ordinary tests of the zone will hit it
Neither — never use stops
3.6R, but with double size
quiz.why: A ratio means little if the stop is inside the range price normally explores. A smaller ratio with a correctly placed stop is the better trade.

quiz.q: Where should the target for a long from support usually be?
options: The far edge of the next resistance zone
The near edge of the next resistance zone that scores 4 or more
Exactly 3R, whatever the map says
The all-time high
quiz.why: Price often reacts as soon as it reaches the next meaningful zone. Targeting the near edge respects where the opposing orders begin.

quiz.q: £10,000 account, 1% risk, 40-pip stop, about £8 per pip per standard lot. Roughly what size?
options: 0.03 lots
0.31 lots
1.25 lots
3.1 lots

quiz.q: A valid trigger offers 27 pips to the next resistance for 33 pips of risk. What do you do?
options: Take it — the trigger is clean
Move the stop to 15 pips to fix the ratio
Skip it — about 0.8R is below the 1.5R minimum
Target the far edge of the resistance zone instead
quiz.why: The stop and target come from the map. If they produce under 1.5R, the trade does not fit, however clean the trigger.

quiz.q: Your support zone sits just above 1.2500. Where is the worst place for your long stop?
options: At 1.2497, just under the round number
At 1.2482, clearly beyond the round number
Beyond the trigger's wick plus a buffer
Beyond the zone's far edge
quiz.why: Stops crowd just beyond round numbers, and those clusters attract overshoots. Push your stop clearly past the figure.

lessons.title: Capstone — The Complete Zone-Trading Playbook
lessons.summary: Run the whole method end to end — map, score, plan, trigger, manage and review — and follow three complete worked trades, including a loser.
lessons.html:
You now have every piece. Why levels exist. How to draw them as zones. How to find the ones that matter, rank them, and read what price does at them: rejection, break, flip, false break. How to enter on evidence, where the stop goes, where the target goes, and when the arithmetic says no.

This final lesson puts the pieces in order. It is written as a playbook: a sequence you can follow every week and every trade, so that your decisions come from the same process whether you are calm, bored, excited or annoyed. After the playbook come three complete worked trades — two winners and a loser — then the strategy passport and the full pre-trade checklist.

As throughout the course, every chart here is an illustrative training chart, and every figure is for teaching. None of it is a recommendation to trade anything.

The playbook in five stages

Stage 1 — Map (weekly, when calm)

Once a week, at a fixed time when you are not looking for a trade:

  1. Glance at the weekly chart. Note one or two standing extremes.
  2. On the daily chart, look back six to twelve months. Mark wick-to-body zones at obvious swing points only.
  3. Merge overlaps. Cull to three to seven zones within reach of current price.
  4. Refine the zones nearest to price on the 4-hour.
  5. Label every zone with its reason in a few words.
  6. Archive dead zones: decisively broken and retested, or passed through twice without reaction.

Stage 2 — Score (weekly, before price arrives)

Score each zone out of 8: departure (0–2), freshness (0–2), timeframe (0–2), independent confluence (0–2). Write the score on the label.

  • 6–8: prime — plan for it in advance.
  • 4–5: working — tradeable with a clean trigger.
  • 0–3: background — a target or obstacle, never an entry.

Stage 3 — Plan (daily, for zones price could reach)

For each prime or working zone that price could reach in the next day or two, write a short if-then plan:

  • If price reaches the zone and a defined trigger closes, then I enter.
  • My stop will be beyond the zone and the trigger extreme, plus a buffer of x pips.
  • My target is the near edge of the next scored zone at y.
  • If that cannot give 1.5R, I will not trade it.
  • Scenario B: if price closes decisively through the zone instead, I will watch for a retest of it in its new role.

Writing scenario B matters. It stops you from being emotionally married to one outcome, and it turns a broken level into the next opportunity instead of a frustration.

Stage 4 — Trigger and execute

When price reaches a planned zone, drop one timeframe and wait for one of the three triggers: pin bar, engulfing candle or strong reclaim close. When one closes within definition, run the checklist at the end of this lesson. Every box ticked: enter, place the stop, place the target, size the position to your fixed risk. Any box unticked: no trade.

Stage 5 — Manage and review

  • Do not move the stop further away. Ever.
  • Tighten the stop only to a new structural point beyond the zone, never to breakeven by reflex.
  • Leave the target where the map put it.
  • After the trade closes, journal it: the zone and its score, the trigger, entry, stop, target, result in R, a screenshot, and one sentence on whether you followed the process.

Review the journal monthly. The questions that matter are about process: which zone scores produced your best and worst trades, which triggers you took outside definition, how often you skipped valid trades or took invalid ones.

Step 1 in practice: the map

Worked trade 1: a rejection long at prime support

The setup. EUR/USD, 4-hour execution from a daily map. A support zone at 1.0800–1.0824 scores 7: sharp departure (2), fresh (2), daily (2), the 1.0800 whole figure inside it (1). The next working resistance sits at 1.0900–1.0922.

The plan, written beforehand. If price reaches 1.0800–1.0824 and a bullish trigger closes on the 4-hour, buy. Stop below the zone and trigger plus 8 pips. Target 1.0898, just under resistance. Minimum 1.5R.

Execution. The pin bar met every part of the definition: lower wick 20 pips against a body of 8, close in the upper fifth, wick into the zone, close inside it. Entry 1.0824 on the close. Stop 1.0788 — below the wick at 1.0796 and the zone's floor at 1.0800, with a buffer. That is 36 pips of risk. With 1% risk on a £10,000 account (illustrative), £100 ÷ (36 pips × about £8 per pip per lot) ≈ 0.35 lots. Target 1.0898: 74 pips, about 2.1R.

Management. Nothing to do. Price left the zone immediately — the behaviour you hope for after a trigger. The stop stayed where it was until a higher low formed well above the zone; the trader could have tightened to below that, but the target was reached first.

Journal line. "Prime support (7), pin bar in definition, 2.1R planned, 2.1R achieved. Process followed."

Worked trade 2: break, retest, short

The setup. GBP/USD, 1-hour execution. A support zone at 1.2650–1.2668 held twice, then broke with a large close and fell 90 pips. That made it a candidate flip zone: it mattered before (two clear holds), the break was decisive, and price travelled well away. The next support sits at 1.2550–1.2570, from the low of the breakdown.

The plan. If price rallies back to 1.2650–1.2668 for the first time and a bearish trigger closes, sell. Stop above the zone plus 8 pips. Target 1.2572, just above the next support. Minimum 1.5R.

Execution. The engulfing candle opened at the previous candle's close, swallowed its body and closed 14 pips below the zone, in the bottom of its range. Entry 1.2636. Stop 1.2676 — above the zone's ceiling at 1.2668 with an 8-pip buffer, also above the trigger's high. Risk 40 pips. Target 1.2572: 64 pips, 1.6R. Acceptable, and no more than that.

Why 1.6R was still worth taking. The temptation is to aim lower — "it will probably break the next support too." Perhaps. But the map said the next crowd of buyers sat at 1.2550–1.2570, and the plan said target the near edge. The target is the map's answer, not your hope.

Journal line. "Working flip zone (6), first retest, engulfing in definition, 1.6R planned and achieved. Process followed."

Worked trade 3: the loser

The setup. USD/JPY, 4-hour. A support zone at 150.00–150.20 scored 6. Price pushed below it with a full close, then the next candle reclaimed strongly — a large bullish body closing back above the zone. The next resistance sat at 151.10–151.30.

The plan. Reclaim long if the reclaim is strong. Stop below the spike low plus a buffer. Target 151.06, just under resistance. Minimum 1.5R.

Execution. The reclaim candle was textbook: a 40-pip body, closing above the zone and above the breakdown candle's open. Entry 150.22. Stop 149.66 — 8 pips below the spike low of 149.74. Risk 56 pips; target 151.06 for 84 pips, exactly 1.5R. The position was sized so 56 pips equalled 1% (illustrative).

What happened. Price made one small push higher, stalled below 150.40, then rolled over. Within about eight candles it had closed below the spike low, taking the stop.

What to learn — and what not to. Look for a process error. The zone was scored before price arrived. The reclaim was within definition. The stop was where the idea was wrong. The target came from the map and passed the minimum. There is no error. The wrong lesson would be "reclaims don't work" or "use tighter stops". The right lesson is the one from Lesson 8: valid trades lose, and fixed risk is what makes that survivable.

There is one useful observation for the journal. After the entry, price stalled instead of leaving the zone — the same hesitation you saw in the failed retest in Lesson 6. It is not an exit signal on its own, but if your journal shows over many trades that stalls like this precede most of your losers, you may later decide to test a rule for it. Test it on your records first; do not invent it after one loss.

Journal line. "Working support (6), strong reclaim in definition, 1.5R planned, −1R result. Process followed. Note: stalled after entry."

The three trades together

Trade Zone score Trigger Planned R Result
1 — EUR/USD long 7 Pin bar 2.1R +2.1R
2 — GBP/USD short 6 Engulfing 1.6R +1.6R
3 — USD/JPY long 6 Reclaim 1.5R −1R

Three trades, chosen to teach, not to represent typical results. In a real sequence the order and mix of winners and losers will be different, and runs of several consecutive losses are normal. What should stay constant is the right-hand column you cannot see here: process followed — yes or no.

Going deeper

Running the method across pairs. One trader can comfortably map four to six pairs a week. More than that and the mapping becomes rushed. Correlated pairs (EUR/USD and GBP/USD, for example) often reach their zones at the same time; treat two correlated trades as close to one larger trade for risk purposes.

When the market is trending hard. In strong trends, counter-trend rejection trades at minor zones fail more often, and break-and-retest trades in the trend's direction tend to work better. Your scorecard's confluence factor already rewards trend structure; you may also choose to trade only with the daily trend until your journal tells you otherwise.

Quiet weeks. Some weeks no planned zone is reached, or no trigger appears. That is not a problem to solve. A method that produces trades every day regardless of conditions is not a zone method.

Measuring yourself. After 30–50 trades, compare your planned R with achieved R, your results by zone score and by trigger type, and how many trades broke a rule. Most traders find that their worst results come from the trades that broke the rules, not from the method itself. That is the most valuable thing a journal can show you.

THE RULES
  • Map weekly when calm; score every zone before price arrives.
  • Trade only prime and working zones, only on a defined trigger, only with at least 1.5R to the next zone.
  • Stop beyond the zone and trigger extreme plus a buffer; size from the stop at a fixed risk.
  • Never widen a stop; never move a target to suit a hope.
  • Journal every trade and judge it on process.

The strategy passport

  • Market: major forex pairs and gold, on a daily map with 4-hour or 1-hour execution.
  • Wait for: price to reach a pre-scored prime (6–8) or working (4–5) zone, or the first retest of a decisively broken zone.
  • Trigger: a pin bar, engulfing candle or strong reclaim close, within definition, at the zone.
  • Stop: beyond the far edge of the zone and the trigger's extreme, plus a buffer, clear of round numbers.
  • Target: the near edge of the next opposing zone scoring 4 or more; minimum 1.5R.
  • Avoid: zones scoring 0–3, triggers away from zones, weak reclaims, chasing breakouts with no retest, and entries just before high-impact news.
PRE-TRADE CHECKLIST
  • The zone is on my weekly map, drawn wick to body, and scored before price arrived
  • The zone scores 4 or more (or it is the first retest of a decisively broken zone that scored 4 or more)
  • A trigger has closed within definition: pin bar, engulfing, or strong reclaim
  • My stop is beyond the zone's far edge and the trigger's extreme, plus a buffer, and clear of any round number
  • My target is the near edge of the next opposing zone scoring 4 or more
  • Reward to target is at least 1.5 times the risk to stop
  • Position size is set so the stop equals my fixed risk per trade
  • No high-impact news is due before the trade has had time to work
  • I can state scenario B — what I will do if the zone breaks instead

Summary

  • The playbook runs in five stages: map, score, plan, trigger and execute, manage and review.
  • Plans are written before price arrives, including a scenario B for a break.
  • Worked trades 1 and 2 show the rejection and the retest done by the book; trade 3 shows a valid trade losing 1R.
  • The passport and checklist are the whole method on one page. Use them every time.
  • Judge yourself on process. Over enough trades, that is the only thing you control.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the playbook's stages?
options: Trigger, map, score, plan, review
Map, score, plan, trigger and execute, manage and review
Score, trigger, map, review, plan
Plan, trigger, map, score, review
quiz.why: Location comes first (map and score), then the written plan, then evidence (trigger), then management and review.

quiz.q: Why does the plan include a 'scenario B'?
options: To have an excuse after a loss
To prepare for a decisive break, so a failed level becomes the next opportunity rather than a frustration
Because every trade needs two entries
To double the position size
quiz.why: Writing what you will do if the zone breaks stops you being married to one outcome and points you to the flip-and-retest setup.

quiz.q: In worked trade 2, why was the target 1.2572 rather than lower?
options: Because 1.6R is the maximum allowed
Because the map showed the next support beginning around 1.2570, and targets go to the near edge of the next zone
Because the trader felt nervous
Because the stop was too wide
quiz.why: The target is the map's answer. Aiming beyond the next zone asks the market to push through opposing orders to reward you.

quiz.q: Worked trade 3 lost 1R. What process error caused the loss?
options: The stop was too tight
The reclaim was weak
There was no process error; it was a valid trade that lost
The zone was not scored
quiz.why: Zone scored in advance, trigger within definition, stop where the idea failed, target from the map, 1.5R. Valid trades sometimes lose.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT on the pre-trade checklist?
options: Reward of at least 1.5R
Stop beyond the zone and trigger extreme plus a buffer
At least three confirming indicators
No high-impact news due before the trade can work
quiz.why: This method uses zones, candle triggers and the map. Indicators are not part of the checklist.

quiz.q: After 40 trades, which journal finding is most useful?
options: Your single biggest winner
How your results differ between trades that followed the process and trades that broke a rule
Which day of the week you felt most confident
How many pips you made in total
quiz.why: Comparing rule-following trades with rule-breaking ones shows whether your problem is the method or the execution — usually the latter.
